description: Urban / soilless / controlled-environment ag (CEA) terminology and funder language. Drawn from USDA Office of Urban Agriculture, NIFA SCRI, FDA Produce Safety Rule, and EPA brownfield-remediation guidance. Starter pack — extend as Tilth handles real urban-ag deployments.

facts.statement: Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA) covers four canonical system types: hydroponics (soilless, water-borne nutrients — NFT, DWC, ebb-and-flow, drip), aquaponics (fish-waste-fed plant systems, RAS-coupled), aeroponics (root-mist nutrient delivery), and soil-based indoor (containerized media in greenhouse). Vertical farming is a *form factor*, not a system type — any of the above can be vertically stacked.

Indoor / supplemental-lighting claims should use PPFD (photosynthetic photon flux density, μmol/m²/s) as the primary metric, not PAR (photosynthetically active radiation, broader band). DLI (daily light integral, mol/m²/day) integrates PPFD over photoperiod. Reviewers flag claims using lumens or lux for plant growth — those are human-vision units.

Hydroponic systems typically use 70-95% less water than equivalent field production, but this is *blue-water* savings — total water-use including condensate handling and evaporative-cooling makeup is lower (~60-90%) but not zero. Recirculating systems lose water primarily to transpiration. Cite Barbosa et al. (2015) for peer-reviewed lettuce comparison; avoid uncited >95% claims.

CEA enables year-round production cycles independent of climate — typical leafy greens cycle is 28-35 days seed-to-harvest with continuous overlapping cohorts. Year-round framing is reviewer-favored when paired with food-security or food-desert outcomes; avoid framing as 'climate-controlled' (sounds energy-intensive) — prefer 'precision environmental management.'

USDA Office of Urban Agriculture and Innovative Production (OUAIP, est. 2020) administers two competitive grants: Urban Agriculture and Innovative Production (UAIP) competitive grants — Planning Projects (up to $75K) and Implementation Projects (up to $300K). Eligible applicants include nonprofits, schools, local governments, tribal governments. Federally recognized Tribes and tribal organizations receive priority.

USDA NIFA Specialty Crop Research Initiative (SCRI) is the primary federal research grant for CEA-relevant work — multi-state, multi-disciplinary projects with industry match (50% non-federal). Recent SCRI awards have funded hydroponic disease management, vertical-farm energy optimization, and CEA cultivar breeding. Match can include in-kind from research partners.

USDA Specialty Crop Block Grant Program (SCBGP) explicitly includes mushrooms as an eligible specialty crop. Mushroom production (button, oyster, shiitake, lion's mane) qualifies for SCBGP-funded marketing, food-safety, and pest-management projects. Indoor / urban mushroom operations are SCBGP-eligible regardless of soilless growing medium.

FDA Produce Safety Rule (under FSMA) applies to most CEA growers producing fresh fruits and vegetables for human consumption, with exemptions for operations under $25K average annual produce sales (small-farm rule) and for produce 'rarely consumed raw.' Hydroponic and aquaponic operations are subject to water testing requirements (21 CFR 112 Subpart E) — frame compliance plan in any urban-ag grant proposal involving direct-to-consumer sales.

Justice40 Initiative (Executive Order 14008) directs 40% of federal climate / clean-energy / sustainable-housing benefits flow to disadvantaged communities. Urban-ag projects sited in DAC-designated census tracts (verifiable via CEJST tool) carry priority points in OUAIP, UAIP, CFP, and many EPA grants. Always cite the specific census tract + CEJST pathway in the project narrative.

USDA still uses 'food desert' terminology (low-income, low-access census tracts >1mi from supermarket urban / >10mi rural). Community-rooted reviewers (NEA, NEH, some equity-focused USDA program officers) increasingly prefer 'food apartheid' — frames the issue as systemic disinvestment, not natural geography. Match the dialect to the funder: USDA reviewers expect 'food desert,' progressive-philanthropy reviewers expect 'food apartheid.' Both are precise; neither is universally correct.

Urban field-scale ag projects on previously-built parcels must address EPA brownfield + soil-lead screening. Pre-production soil testing (EPA Method 3050B for total Pb) is reviewer-expected; results above 400 ppm (residential / play-area threshold) require remediation plan or raised-bed-with-imported-soil framing. Cite EPA RSL tables. Soilless / hydroponic operations on contaminated parcels sidestep the issue but reviewers want explicit acknowledgment.

USDA defines 'beginning farmer or rancher' (BFR) as having operated a farm/ranch ≤10 years. Urban-ag programs particularly value BFR participation given the pipeline-creation framing. BFRDP (Beginning Farmer and Rancher Development Program) is the dedicated training grant; OUAIP UAIP and CFP both score BFR-serving projects higher. SDA + BFR overlap (socially-disadvantaged + beginning) compounds priority.

relationships.description: Hydroponic and aquaponic systems specifically fall under FSMA Produce Safety Rule water-testing requirements.
Hydroponic system definition supports the 70-95% blue-water savings claim.
Justice40 designation adds priority points to OUAIP UAIP applications.
BFR + SDA + Justice40-DAC-tract triple-overlap is the strongest priority-points stack for urban-ag grants.
